title: Credit Cycles
subfield: Macro-Finance / Collateral Constraints and Business Cycles
datasets: None (theoretical paper; illustrative numerical simulation only)
research_question: In an economy where debt must be secured by durable, productive collateral, how large and how persistent are the responses of asset prices, investment and output to a small, temporary shock, and can the interaction between debt and collateral generate cycles on its own?
main_finding: Because the collateral asset's price capitalizes the entire expected future path of credit-constraint tightness, the dynamic multiplier on asset prices exceeds the static multiplier by a factor equal to the inverse of the net real interest rate; a temporary 1% shock generates land-price and output responses of comparable size to the shock, persisting roughly a decade, and lumpy investment can generate damped, multi-year predator-prey cycles between debt and landholding.
research_gaps: No priced credit risk: lenders are risk-neutral, so the model speaks to credit quantities, not credit spreads
No theory of who becomes credit-constrained or when
Mechanism not robust to hedging markets against the aggregate shock (Krishnamurthy 2003)
Purely deterministic, one-time shock; authors flag a fully stochastic extension as the 'pressing next step'
research_ideas: Solve a fully stochastic, globally-solved version of the model with recurring, anticipated shocks
Test the lumpy-investment build-up prediction against farm- or firm-level micro data
Endogenize the supply of hedging instruments to restore amplification and generate a priced credit spread
Cross-country test of the elasticity threshold separating cyclical from monotonic collateral dynamics
Horse race between collateral-constraint and heterogeneous-beliefs explanations of asset-price overshooting
